utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-08-91-T the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, all, and may I have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, Belinda Pidwell, Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic and Slobodan Cvijetic for Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic for Mr. Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I just say that with the consent of the Defence we are going to interpose the witness who should have come later this week. He has domestic problems which mean that he couldn't hang on as we anticipate the witness Mr. Djeric is likely to take a very long time so we hope that Your Honours won't mind we're interposing that witness. He will need -- he's got protective measures, and I think it's image and pseudonym, so we'll have to adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We will not have to adjourn because it's just image.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is it? Oh, right. Sorry, my fault. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: There's no objection on protective measures from Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is entering, I tried my best to group the documents as instructed by the Trial Chamber. I managed that, and I grouped them in five different groups. One is instructions and rule books. The second one are the instruction concerning detention and the facilities. The third group is documents concerning MUP members who committed crimes, which we discussed before. The fourth is information requests. The fifth is war crimes instructions, and the last is instructions concerning the looting. Looting, looting of the property and other crimes committed by members of the MUP. Now, the problem, unfortunately, Your Honours, is with the -- with the e-court. I was thinking about it. The point of the matter is that only one document can be shown on the -- on the monitor at a certain point in time, so I will anyhow need to go document by document. I will try to keep it at a very fast pace, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Our proposal is that if you show us one document from each group, say the most important document from each group, and if you assert that the other documents in that group are the same or more or less the same, and if the Prosecution doesn't object then I think we have a look at one document and we have that admitted along with the two or three or four other documents in that group. I don't know if that is acceptable to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Just to suggest some way of binding the Chamber's need to actually have a look at least some of the documents and the quest for expediency.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand Your Honour's wish, but let me just give you one example. For example, one of the instructions concerns the reporting, the need for reporting which the witness talked about during the direct examination. So daily reporting, monthly, three months and a year reporting. There is an instruction on that. So that's one thing. But also there is an instruction on the disciplinary responsibility of the members of MUP which is clearly very important. Now, I can -- I can show the instruction on the -- the rule-book on disciplinary responsibility during the time of imminent threat of war, but I don't know how is that connected with the -- with the instruction on the reporting. That is the only problem that I have in that respect, Your Honours. But if -- if the Trial Chamber pleases, that way we can do it. And if Ms. Korner doesn't object, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't mind at all. I mean, if I'm given a list of the documents that have been provided to us and shown what -- you know, what categories they go into, rather like the ones we did for Mr. Djeric, then I don't require the witness to simply say, "Yes, I recognise this," if that's all that's going to be asked. But obviously if you want to ask -- if the implementation personally by the witness is going to be sought, well, then obviously the document will have to be looked at.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I definitely need the implementation from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think we will save time, Your Honours, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That just occurred to me that the whole administrative back and forth in terms of how to do it, we'll probably spent as much time as we would have had gone through them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Such is life, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I begin, good morning, Mr. Krulj.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday I showed you the witness document 1D2436. The witness commented on the document, but due to lack of time I omitted to tender it into evidence. This is the instruction on reporting, the document I just mentioned a minute ago. [In English] May I have -- yes, I'm waiting for the Trial Chamber to -- I think the document has been commented, and I offer it for evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: My apologies, Mr. Zecevic. Marked and entered -- entered and marked, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D51, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. The next document that I would like to put to the witness, and can it please be shown on the screen, is 1D5393. This is a mandatory instruction on the procedure by the Ministry of the Interior when conducting searching activities, and this is 1D5393.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What number is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I can't help you any longer because I had to group these documents, but this is the mandatory instruction by the Ministry of the Interior when conducting searching activities. It will come up on the screen. Mr. Krulj, this instruction pertains to searching activities when they are searching for perpetrators who at the time when the criminal report was made were not available to law enforcement organs; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And this instruction sets out a certain procedure on to how this needs to be done, what are the deadlines for wanted notices and so on.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is from October 1992. And while you worked as chief of public security station in Ljubinje, I suppose that you applied this instruction.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But until the instruction was issued, until it came down from the MUP of Republika Srpska in October 1992, until that time you applied the instruction that was in force for the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and it's almost completely identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have this document tendered into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D52, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now can we show the witness 1D00-3727.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is instruction for drafting annual reports, and this instruction is linked to the previous document, the previous exhibit -- rather, the first one we mentioned this morning, which is called Instruction on urgent current occasional and statistical reporting within the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm so sorry to interrupt. I was distracted by something else when Mr. Zecevic produced the document. I haven't got a translation. I didn't see one on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I'm so sorry. I'm so sorry. This is because of the fast pace I'm going. There is one of the other documents which is still pending translation. So if we can have it MFI'd, and we will offer it for evidence once the translation is -- is received. I'm really sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I have no reason to doubt it is what you say it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, it was sent to CLSS some time ago, but it hasn't been as yet translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So that the document should -- that document should now be marked for identification rather than --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] that is correct, Your Honour, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D52 will be marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm really sorry for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krulj, were you able to find 1D3727, which is the instruction on drafting annual reports? You have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you see this? This was sent to everybody, CSBs, to everybody, to SJBs, to everybody. You received this document?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you write your annual report for 1992 on the basis of this document?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D53, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown 65 ter document 242.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is the document that has a cover letter of the 19th of September, 1992, and these are the rules on the disciplinary responsibility of the workers of the Ministry of the Interior under the wartime regimen once the immediate threat of war has been declared. You see that document?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with these rules?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: There are just two or three things that I wish to ask you from this -- these rules. These rules shorten the procedure for establishing disciplinary responsibility of the workers of the MUP; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Disciplinary proceedings are regulated by law, the Law on Internal Affairs and by the rules on disciplinary proceedings in peacetime. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Once an immediate threat of war is declared and once the wartime regimen of work is introduced -- was introduced, it became necessary to adopt these rules on the disciplinary responsibility in order to be more efficient in ensuring the discipline among the workers of MUP. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, would you please look at Article 2. Page 3 in the Serbian. It's 0324-6179 in Serbian. That's the ERN number in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the English text as well, Article 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Article 2, which we can see is continued, is carried over on page 3, enumerates serious violations of duty by the members of the interior, the additional ones that were envisioned for this wartime regimen; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At the very beginning, I think the third bullet point -- so this is Article 2, on the third page, on the following page, please. So from the above, the third bullet point it says: "Committing a crime for dishonourable motives." Could you tell us what would that be, a crime for dishonourable motives? What would be the elements of that crime?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a crime for dishonourable motives could be of -- a crime of a sexual nature or gaining material gain, profit from a victim.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, from a victim. All right. And right underneath that the next bullet point: "Expressing national, racial, or religious intolerance and acting against the defence measures and against the security interests of the state." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And in addition to this there were also grave violations of work duty which could be penalised by terminating somebody, which is the most serious consequence that could be pronounced as a result of a disciplinary proceedings. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters. I'm speaking quite fast, and I think on page 9, line 18, I think what we discussed is the termination of work. That's the term.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see last page, Article 17, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Article 17, please look at it. Do you remember that article?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Article 17 of these rules says that the statute of limitations for conducting disciplinary proceedings is extended.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for light violations three months from the day that they learned about the violation, and for grave violations the deadline was extended by six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And then these rules extended doubly. So for light violations it was extended from three months to six months, and for grave violations from six months to one year. That's what it says here; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 3, if the violation of work duty also had elements of a crime, then the institution of disciplinary proceedings would run out, the statute of limitations would run out one year after the day that they learned about such a violation.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that these rules on disciplinary responsibility are much stricter -- provided for much stricter rules concerning the disciplinary responsibility of the members of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to making the rules much stricter, the statute of limitations was also extended so that -- so as to avoid that a violation that was made would be unpunished due to the fact that there was a war going on and there was an immediate threat of war declared and so on; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this document admitted, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D54.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have now completed this group of documents which are rules and instructions, and now we're going to move to documents that refer to rules on detention and -- and custody, and can we please look at 1D00-264.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 2764, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you see on the monitor this is an order from the MUP of the Republika Srpska of the 10th of August, 1992, and it was sent to all the CSBs, and you will see at the bottom of the page it has also been sent to some public security stations. Did you directly receive this document, or are you familiar with it by means of the order that you received from the CSB of Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the custom was that some of the documents that arrived at the centre only are copied and then dispatched in the form of an order to the public security stations, and public security stations usually received all of these orders through the CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You can see under item 1 that the order deals with detention and holding measures that are to be applied exclusively within existing regulations. Do you see that? That --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So that means that the detention and holding measures can be enforced only within the bounds provided for under the law.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the next paragraph it sayings that the CSB chiefs are personally responsible for the lives of the persons during detention and custody and are responsible to prevent any kind of abuse in that area.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the third, it says that they have to fulfil the basic hygiene and health requirements at the premises where those persons are being held; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 2 talks about the security of collection centres, and it says that the security collection centres are under the direct responsibility of the Serbian Army and issues the instructions that if the army didn't have enough manpower it shall therefore be necessary to engage members of the reserve police pursuant to the laws that we discussed yesterday. So they would become part of the army forces at that time in order to carry out the security duties in these collection centres; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, could you elicit from the witness how he distinguishes between detention centres and collection centres? Why is there this difference between the responsibility of the CSB on -- for the first group and for the Serbian Army for the second group?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me clarify. Paragraph 1 of the order refers to measures of detention and holding. The detention and holding measures are measures that you, under the Law on Criminal Procedure and the Law on Internal Affairs, exercise as part of your regular police duties; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They are applied to perpetrators of criminal act, and they can be held for up to a period of three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And these collection centres, this is a term that does not exist in the Law on Criminal Procedure, and the police has no jurisdiction either under the Law on Criminal Procedure or the Law on Internal Affairs or any other law over such premises, collection centres.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. But I do not differentiate between detention and collection centres. Even I don't know what that is. I mean, is that the same thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I did not encounter any detention centres in this document. I didn't -- in paragraph 1, what is being mentioned is detention and holding measures or custody, and then in paragraph 2 we have the secure -- the collection centres. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are two separate concepts, terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your territory you did not have --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The public security station in Ljubinje did not have any collection centres, did it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know how far we can get with this witness on this matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please tender this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D55, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the witness document 65 ter 217. It's from the same group of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a dispatch from the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the 17th of August, 1992, to the public security centres and refers once again to the order to act pursuant -- to act -- or the conduct towards prisoners of war, refugees, civilian population. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the contents of this document?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This document is an order that prisoners of war, the civilian population, and refugees should be treated exclusively according to the law within the framework of the MUP jurisdiction and according to the war on international conventions which replace the subject matter.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the norms regulating that particular area?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 2 says: "The ministry shall immediately be informed of the existence of public outlaw, rogue prisons, camp and the treatment of persons of war or refugees that are being held there." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the last paragraph says that with regard to persons who do not comply with valid regulations, it says it is necessary, the last sentence, to immediately start gathering information and documentation and submit criminal reports to the authorised prosecutor's office. Is this in accordance with the legal authorities of the MUP and the regular procedures --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- to which the law obliges you to?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obliges us to, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you act -- in cases like this -- did you have cases like this?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But you are familiar with these regulations?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D56, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We will look at the last document from this group, 1D00-197. It's a dispatch of the 24th of August, 1992, from the MUP, dispatched to the CSBs and the PJ -- and the SJBs. Do you remember that document?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2 -- or, actually, we can see from the document that the dispatch was a consequence of a request of the Ministry for Labour and Social Affairs of Republika Srpska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And once again it refers to these illegal, irregular collection centres, camps, and the like. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Internal Affairs is placing you on notice that regardless of the jurisdiction you would need to furnish the data, meaning that even though you were not the person of jurisdiction authorised for such collection centres, you were obliged to report all that you know and report of the existence of such places if you were aware of that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I think we need to make a comment here about jurisdiction in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can -- actually, when I was reading this document last night, it says regardless of the jurisdiction. So we did jobs that were not in our jurisdiction, that is true. So I think that in this case, not only in relation to this document but generally, it's important to clarify the manner in which the civilian police was authorised for military conscripts that had committed criminal act. I think that the Prosecution and the Defence are asking questions about the military prosecution organs, military courts and so on. So the army worked according to the laws of the federal state. So we had no jurisdiction over military matters. I am only talking about this in order to protect the reputation and the work of members of the police who I believe did their jobs as honourably as they were able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, but you spoke a little bit fast, so for purposes of the transcript I would like to say the following: I think on page 17, lines 3 and 4 -- or lines 2 and 3, you said something slightly different than what is in the transcript. I'm going to clarify. You did not have any jurisdiction over members of the military; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So members of the military were absolutely under the jurisdiction of military investigative and judicial organs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now go back to the document. This document obliged you to furnish the following information: The name of the place where the detention camp, prison, or collection centre was located; the name of the municipality; then who ordered the institution to be established; who gave the order for those people to be brought to the detention camps; the number of imprisoned people or captured people and their particulars; as well as the number of persons arrested and their particulars. So you were given the deadline until the 30th of August of that year to furnish this information. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the document?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Since in your territory you didn't have such instances, I assume that there was no reason for you to act upon this order.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether you informed the ministry that there were no such centres in the Municipality of Ljubinje?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were obliged also to reply in the negative. This was part of our duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D57.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please look at 65 ter 125.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a dispatch of the Banja Luka CSB of May 15th, 1992, which is conveying to its public security stations under its jurisdiction the text of the order received from the MUP, and this is why I am using this. I am sure that you did not see the dispatch in this form, but the text was conveyed from the ministry order. So I assume that you also found out about it through your CSB centre. Do you remember a dispatch with these contents?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't get this. This is Banja Luka. I cannot remember it right now. Perhaps we did receive it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This again deals with the information about inadequate, unprincipled conduct of some members of the reserve forces, and the document takes the position that such persons cannot be members of the MUP, which is something that we discussed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The centre probably did have this dispatch, but this matter is covered by a number of documents, so I really cannot remember in detail this particular one. I think all the stations in the area of Republika Srpska received a dispatch like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the idea of showing you this document actually is something that was done constantly. This is the earliest one that I managed to find of May 15th, but documents and orders of this content were re-issued periodically throughout the entire 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not sure if I should tender this or not because the witness was unable to recognise the document. I'm not going to tender that particular document then. Next document, please, 65 ter 185.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This document comes from the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska, dated 23rd of July, 1992. You have it on your monitor. This is an order that came as a result of the conclusions of that first collegium of the MUP of Republika Srpska which you attended on the 11th of July in Belgrade. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This document is from the same group of documents. This order pertains to procedure that needs to be applied in relation to MUP members who committed crimes either earlier or during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You can see here that the ministry is ordering you that in relation to such members who have committed criminal acts before or since the beginning of the war, in other words, since the formation of the MUP of Republika Srpska, that you need to take legal measures with respect of such members -- against such members. When they say legal measures, or measures provided under the law, do you mean -- do you read this to mean both criminal measures and disciplinary measures?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand it as both of those measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And then in item 2 they say the chiefs of CSBs are responsible for implementing the order?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And then in item 3, the ministry required that information be delivered to them by a certain date.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this order?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D58.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Another document on the following day. This is 65 ter 188. Could we have that on our screens? This is the document of the ministry dated the 24th of July, which is to say on the following day after the order that we just saw, which was dated 23rd of July, and this here is dated 24th of July. On behalf of the minister somebody else signed the document, and it pertains to an identical situation, namely that members of the ministry against whom criminal proceedings were underway before responsible courts need to be relieved of duty and placed immediately at the disposal of the Army of Republika Srpska. Do you remember this document?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So this is yet another document from the series of documents which all kept reiterating the same matter throughout 1992, from the very beginning?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have this document tendered into evidence as well too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, just for clarification, these orders, do they imply that -- that persons who were under prosecution for having committed crimes were being released from the prisons and put under the army's command?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I believe that we have clarified this yesterday --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Shouldn't the witness answer rather than Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Naturally. Naturally. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krulj, please.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the Ministry of the Interior who were criminally prosecuted and against whom criminal proceedings are being instituted before the competent courts of Republika Srpska should be relieved of duty and placed at the disposal of the army. This has nothing to do with criminal responsibility. That is to say, a policeman who made a violation earlier and criminal proceedings were instituted against him or he just committed a violation or a crime against him, criminal report would be submitted to the relevant prosecutor's office. And in addition to that, in addition to criminal or disciplinary responsibility, in addition to that, he needed to be relieved of duty. He needed to be suspended from his regular police duties and placed at the disposal of the army. I think I explained that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But would he be released from custody and transferred to combat activities, for instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. If he was in detention, then no. If he committed a crime, a criminal report is filed against him, just like any other citizen. A report is filed with the relevant prosecutor's office. And simultaneously, he is suspended from his police duties. So these are additional measures. And proceedings are instituted against him regardless of where he is, be it in the army or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes. I think my problem is that I'm not sure I fully understand the link between being under investigation or prosecution and then the transfer to the army. Suppose a policeman had committed a crime and was being prosecuted for that, and he was not held in detention in relation to the crime that he committed. That the order apparently says that this policeman would then be relieved of his duty, so he would no longer be able to work as a policeman, and then he would be put to the army, I suppose to be enrolled in the army as a soldier, and that's the link that I'm not sure I understand. Can you explain why was it that some policemen who had committed crimes and were under prosecution were then not only relieved of their police duties but also forced into the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we look at the rules on disciplinary responsibility of the members of the MUP, then you will see that there are light violations and grave violations. A grave violation would be a commission of a crime. A disciplinary proceeding is independent of any criminal proceeding, and in those cases these people were mostly disciplined by terminating them at work for the crime they had committed regardless of what was the outcome of the criminal trial for that crime, and that person was terminated at work as a result of disciplinary proceedings. That person would automatically be called up by a military organ to enlist him in the army. I hope that this is entirely clear, but if necessary, I will clarify more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So if I may add on to this in order to assist further. So a military duty to participate in the defence of the country is the highest duty according to the law and the constitution, and it is a duty of every individual within a certain age range. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And in that sense everybody has a duty and an obligation to defend their country.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When a person is a member of the MUP, then that person carries out that duty to defend via performing their duties within the Ministry of the Interior as their work obligation.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Since in May a general mobilisation was declared -- do you remember that? It was declared in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Then the person whose work duty within the organs of MUP ceased to exist as a result of the gravest punishment, as a result of being terminated at work, then that person automatically is converted into a conscript and sent to the front.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So this is a legislative, automatic process. It is not just a result of this order by the Ministry of the Interior. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope this is clear, but if the Court wishes me, I can provide further clarification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just one more matter. If a criminal report, a criminal complaint was filed against that person who committed a crime, a criminal report to the authorised prosecutor, the outcome of that criminal report will be decided by the prosecutor and not by the chief of that organ of the interior. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now show to the witness 1D00-4597.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, the registry reminds me the last document hasn't yet been admitted. So you're tendering that as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, by all means, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D59, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 1D00-4597, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krulj, this document was issued by the Ministry of the Interior in Bijeljina, dated 16 November 1992. It was sent to chiefs of all public security stations and chiefs of all CSBs. Do you remember receiving this document?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can see that here, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This document, first of all, pertains to the conclusions of the collegium held by the minister of the interior on the 5th of November when current problems in the work of the ministry were discussed.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please go to the last page. This document mostly deals with personnel issues, most of the document. And please go to the last page, item 9, which is on page 3 of your text. Item 9.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So item 9 again orders the same thing as the previous order dated the 23rd of July, namely that those persons who had been held criminally responsible for crimes or who had committed crimes or in some other way compromised themselves need to be excluded from the ranks of the Ministry of the Interior. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have this document tendered into evidence as well, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D60.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 65 ter 356. Could you scroll up, please, so that the witness can see the signature. Rather, scroll down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This document is dated 15 April 1992, Ministry of the Interior. It's an order. You see the order?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. We had similar orders. They would come in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: See what it says here. It has only two items. Item 1 says: "Persons committing seizure, looting, appropriation of other people's and missing property and other unauthorised acts in order to achieve unlawful gain are to be identified and subjected to the most rigorous responsibility measures, including arrest and detention. "This order shall come into force immediately." Tell me, please, this order actually just additionally highlights your duty under the law?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it does so for the umpteenth time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you apply this order in your work, this order and the law?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To the extent that we were able to, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we introduce this into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krulj, was this a frequent occurrence that you had to arrest and detain and prosecute and ensure prosecution of policemen in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We didn't understand each other. We often received orders of this kind, and perhaps there were just two or three such cases over a period of two or three years. But we frequently received orders of this type. You can see yourself that the documents repeat themselves. This is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand that, that these orders came frequently. My curiosity was just in relation to your answer that you did in fact apply this provision. So I was curious to know how frequent that happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps several times. I cannot remember how many times there was the case of somebody from the police looting or stealing or something, and then this kind of report would be issued. But this was not the case in my jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Just one clarification while we still have the document on the screen. This order does not strictly refer to members of the MUP, because it says "persons who commit." So it refers to everyone practically, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The reason to emphasise these duties is due to the fact that on the 15th of April a war broke out and this is why these duties were being emphasised one more time in this order.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise. I thought this just referred to members of the ministry, but what I can see now is that it does say "persons." Things like this were more common. There were lots of confiscated vehicles that had been stolen, a lot of movable items that had been robbed, and these kind of items -- kinds of items were often confiscated at check-points and in town. I apologise again. I thought that this referred exclusively to members of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think now we've clarified the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please tender this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D61.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now move to the next group of documents, and can the witness please be shown document 65 ter 138.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's an order on reporting for the needs of the government. It's a document by the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina of the 26th of May, 1992, and it's sent to all the security services centres, including Trebinje. I assume that via the CSB you were also requested to furnish this information.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 1 of the document, it says that "it's essential to regularly write reports about offences against the people and property within the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina," is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And then after that certain groups of questions are mentioned, and they're more of the nature of statistical information; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And on page 3, if you recall, you'll see that the deadline was set until the 31st of May, 1992. Do you remember if you did send your CSB in Trebinje the data from your public security station?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We probably did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would like to tender this document, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It's admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D62.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're now coming to an important document. It's 1D0609. Can we please show this document to the witness 1D00-0609.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was on, but it wasn't working. I'm sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I'm going to repeat. This is a document of the Ministry of the Internal Affairs of the republic -- of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina of the 19th of July, 1992, and it was sent to the chiefs personally of the security services centres, including the one in Trebinje, and the document is the result of conclusions adopted at a meeting of the first MUP collegium on the 11th of July, 1992, in Belgrade, which you also attended. This document pertains to the tasks to document, and uncover acts of war crimes or genocide and the submission of criminal reports as well as other documents and orders, and for those purposes the administration for administration and management drafted a questionnaire on war crimes and victims of genocide, and then there are instructions on what to do with this questionnaire. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And what the document insists is that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Just a moment. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krulj, could you please look at the third paragraph on the first page which states: "It should be borne in mind that questionnaires on war crimes remain just a form of investigative documentation only, until such time as they have been proven (judicial sentence or decision by an authorised state commission) and will be so regarded, all the more so because criminal reports will also be submitted against unidentified perpetrators." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then the last paragraph states the deadline by which the documents should be provided. What I would like now to do is to look at the actual form, and that is on page 3. That is the form RZ on page 3 of this document. You are familiar with this form, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It was a compulsory form for each individual case of a war crime, and it would be filled in and sent to the Ministry of Internal Affairs. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was done by the criminal police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have cases in your practice where such a form had to be filled in in your territory? I'm talking about 1992.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, no.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we tender this document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D63.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I still have two documents to go through and four or five questions, so I think I will need ten minutes at the most. I can see that it's time for a break, so if I may be allowed to continue for another ten minutes after the break and then I believe that I will complete my cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] almost as bad as mine, but can I just ask. I know that Mr. Krgovic has got questions. We've then got another witness. It doesn't seem to me that we're going to get to Mr. Djeric today. So therefore I'm -- if anybody has any doubts about that, otherwise I'm going to send him away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mrs. Korner, I thought that you had asked that a witness ST-79 would follow --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly. I'm talking about Mr. Djeric. He's here as well. That's the one I want to send away, because I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes. There's no chance that he will begin today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I don't think so either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we'll take the break. We return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, while the witness is in the process of resuming the stand, we have two oral rulings to deliver. Judge Harhoff will deliver one and Judge Delvoie the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. I hope the interpreters have been given a copy so that they could follow.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: On -- I'll read slowly then. On 8 October 2009, the Prosecution filed a notice in relation to 65 ter numbers of additional documents for expert witness Dorothea Hanson in which it requests the Trial Chamber to take note of the addition of seven documents to its exhibit list. The seven documents are all referred to in Dorothea Hanson's expert report. The Prosecution submits that they were disclosed to the Defence no later than February 2008 but that the documents were not included on the exhibit list filed on 8 June 2009 as they are background documents supporting the report. Following the direction of the Trial Chamber given at the Pre-Trial Conference on 4 September 2009, the evidence of Mrs. Hanson is to be heard pursuant to Rule 94 bis, and the Prosecution now wishes to use the seven documents in its examination-in-chief. The Prosecution therefore asks the Trial Chamber to take note of the addition of the seven documents. Once a party has filed its exhibit list pursuant to Rule 65 ter, it can only be amended with leave of the Trial Chamber through a motion showing, among other things, good cause for the request and why the documents are of sufficient importance to justify their inclusion. It is insufficient and inappropriate for a party to merely submit a notice to the Chamber as it wishes to amend its Rule 65 ter lists. In the absence of a properly filed motion, the Chamber notes that Defence is also deprived of an opportunity to respond. While the Chamber will on this occasion and in the interests of judicial economy treat the notices as motions for the amendment of the Prosecution's exhibit list, it will not accept this practice in the future. Any future similar requests are to be made by properly filed motions. The Prosecution does not extend any argument to demonstrate good cause for the addition of these documents to its exhibit list nearly two months after the ruling on the mode of testimony of this witness, nor does it indicate the importance of the documents to the evidence of the witness. As the Prosecution has not established good cause for the relief sought, it is not necessary for the Chamber to seek responses from the Defence in this instance. Consequently, and in view thereof, the Chamber denies the request for amending the Prosecution's exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour -- sorry, before you deal with the next ruling, can I ask this: that if we do a proper filing given reasons why, would Your Honours be prepared to perhaps reconsider? We take -- we take the rebuke seriously, and it won't happen again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, we, of course, don't see that we can prevent you from re-filing, and once you -- we'll have to consider it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: On the 14th of October, 2009, the Prosecutor -- the Prosecution filed a notice requesting the Trial Chamber to take note of the amendments to the mode of testimony of ST-52 and ST-79 from viva voce to Rule 92 ter, and of ST-4 from Rule 92 bis to Rule 92 ter. Furthermore, pursuant to Rule 92 ter, the Prosecution seeks the admission into evidence of the statements and transcripts of these witnesses and associated exhibits which its status forms an inseparable part of the witness's evidence. Fourteen of the documents do not appear on the Prosecution's exhibit list, and the Prosecution therefore seeks to add them to its exhibit list. On the 26th of October, 2009, the Prosecution filed a similar notice requesting the Trial Chamber to take note of the amendment to the mode of testimony of Witness ST-140 from viva voce to Rule 92 ter. The Prosecution also seeks to admit -- to add, sorry, nine associated exhibits to its exhibit list. The Prosecution argues that there is no prejudice to the accused as a result of the variation of the mode of testimony. Prosecution submits that the transcripts, written statements, and associated exhibits of the witnesses meet the requirements of admissibility under the rules and that the amendments are made in an attempt to save time in court and streamline the presentation of evidence at trial. As noted in the preceding decision, the party's exhibit list can only be amended with leave of the Trial Chamber upon a showing of good cause. The same holds true for a party's witness list. Changes to the mode of testimony of witnesses who appear on the witness list are to be made by a properly reasoned motion for the admission of witness statements and transcripts pursuant -- pursuant to the appropriate Rule, that is, either Rule 92 bis or Rule 92 ter. For the reasons noted in the preceding decision, the Chamber emphasises that it is insufficient and inappropriate to a party to merely submit -- submit a notice to the Chamber as it amends its lists. It is also contrary to the guidelines that the Chamber had -- has issued. Nevertheless, in the interest of judicial economy, the Chamber will on this occasion treat the notice -- notices as motions for the admission of evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter. Having so decided, the Trial Chamber grants the Defence 14 days from today to respond in respect of ST-4, ST-52, and ST-140. The Chamber has been informed by way of e-mail from the Prosecution to its legal officers that the Defence agrees that ST-79 be heard after ST-202. I think that is correct. Isn't it, Mr. Zecevic? Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Can the Defence also state whether it objects to the request to her -- to hear, sorry, ST-79 pursuant to Rule 92 ter? Do you object to that, or are you in agreement with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We do not object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You do not object. Mr. Krgovic, you do not object?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: As the Defence does not object, the Trial Chamber allows the Prosecution to call ST-79 pursuant to Rule 92 ter. The Chamber also finds that the three associated documents form an inextricable and indispensable part of this evidence. The Trial Chamber will accept on to the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter exhibit list this prior testimony and the three accompanying documents. This material will be admitted into evidence upon the witnesses having complied with the conditions of Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. A minor point by way of correction. At line 9 on page 36, the transcript correctly says that -- it is insufficient for the Prosecution to submit a notion, but clearly the word we intended to say was notice. Thank you. Could we have the witness back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. While we wait for the witness, I was notified by my assistants that 1D52, which was erroneously offered for evidence and then marked for identification because the translation is pending, has been with the CLSS since 4th of December, 2008. utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, at the -- just before the break you had indicated that you would wrap up in about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.text: I'm only alerting you at this point.

utterances.text: Thank you very much. I will -- I just need to clarify two things and I -- I'm going to be finished in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krulj, thank you very much for this. We have no additional documents. Now I'm interested in some facts, so could you please assist us with that. Were you familiar, back in 1992, with the fact that in Bileca there was some sort of collection centre or a prison or anything of the sort in?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I learned that from conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So from conversations you were aware of the fact that they existed?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And what facts did you learn through those conversations?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I learned that in a room, I don't know whether it was students' hall or something like that, or a public security station room, but I knew that there was a certain number of Muslims there who were held as a result of conflicts in the northern part of Bileca municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This information, did you receive it via official channels, or was it via private channels that you just happened to hear of it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't receive it via official channels but rather via private channels?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. When you say that they were taken into custody, by whom? Was it by the army?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were the military units, and that was the very beginning, so I really don't know who participated in those conflicts and who took those people in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And you don't know who was in charge of law and order of that -- in that collection centre, who was in charge of security?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, you are sure that you did not receive officially, via official channels, any information about any prison or collection centre in Bileca?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to see P162. I think that you saw that document the day before yesterday in examination-in-chief. P162.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is not so important to me. Can we now turn to page 3, please. Page 3 in the Serbian -- or, rather, I apologise, page 5. See in this lower part of the page there's quite a bit that is added, added by hand and by pencil or pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we -- we need the bottom part of the page, please, so could you scroll down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you see that there are things added?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. What is important for me is that there are certain portions that have been added in handwriting in pencil or pen.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC

utterances.text: What I would say that this is some sort of a draft version of the document because it hasn't been signed, and I think that a document that has such added portions, portions that are added so illegibly, could not be sent to some other institution. That is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Krulj. My name is Dragan Krgovic, and on behalf of the Defence of Mr. Zupljanin, I am going to put some questions to you about your testimony over the past couple of days.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krulj, when you talked during the examination-in-chief about the Specijalna Jedinica Policija unit, you mentioned and the Prosecutor showed you a document P169 how this unit was trained at the Bileca barracks. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecutor asked me if they had training. Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And this is the military barracks in Bileca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's the headquarters of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And then you responded to the Prosecutor's question that the unit existed from before; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I assume that if it was trained by the military that it was also issued with weapons by the army and that it took part in combat together with the army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And it probably took part in combat at the time when the conflict broke out; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And members of the unit did not wear police uniforms, but they wore camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they wore camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And red berets, I assume, and maybe some other markings.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember the kind of caps they wore. They didn't wear the police caps in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, I think we have come to understand that camouflage uniforms could be either the colour of the army, or they could be in blue colours so as to indicate somehow that they were police units. Could you clarify with the witness which colour the camouflage uniforms had?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you heard His Honour's question. Could you tell us about the kind of uniform that it was?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mostly saw the military camouflage uniforms in the units, because that was worn by a number of the soldiers, whereas most of the soldiers in Herzegovina were dressed in the old JNA uniforms. Yes. These were green camouflage uniforms. Let me put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I apologise. They were not wearing the blue uniforms.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were not, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krulj, we're going to go back to a different topic now and that's the meeting of the 11th of July, 1992, in Belgrade. From what I understood, the point of the meeting was to provide an opportunity for the chiefs of the CSBs and individuals from the public security station to talk about the problems they were encountering in their work, to report on the situation in their zones where they were located, and to try through the ministry to take certain steps in order to resolve all these matters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You can see that from the minutes of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And each of the participants at the meeting talked about the problems they were encountering and about the most burning issues in the territory covered by a certain SJB or a CSB; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And this was a legitimate legal way to indicate some problem or some occurrence in order to have that matter resolved within the system pursuant to regulations and the laws that were in effect at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The problems that were discussed at the meeting were more or less identical in the entire Republika Srpska territory, with minor deviations here and there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were some deviations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And because of that you were able to form an impression of the situation not only in your own region but in the other regions as well. You were able to get a complete picture; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't remember if the meeting was held in two parts, and I don't remember if we attended the entire meeting, the meeting between the stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to take you back now to the document from that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the witness P160, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if you have that in front of you, but these are the minutes from the meeting. And if you don't have it in front of you, you can just follow it on the screen, and we will show the relevant pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown page 4 of the document in the Serbian, and this is page 7 in the English version. This is ERN number 324-1854. That's the relevant page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, you said that this meeting took place in Belgrade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. And the witness explained yesterday why that meeting was held in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This part that I am referring you to is the address by Mr. Zupljanin, and I'm going to read a part of it. "Paramilitary organising and violent behaviour of a number of armed groups and vast quantities of illegally held weapons in circumstances of ethnic intolerance, chauvinism, and revenge-seeking present a great danger for the law, security of the citizens." Would you agree that the situation was the same where you were?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Zupljanin pointed the problems with the paramilitary forces at this meeting, and as a conclusion of what he says, I would like to show you page 26 in the B/C/S. In the English that would be page --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I think it's page 26 in the English. You can see that conclusion there. Perhaps you can read that part where it says "Activities of the paramilitaries," and, "We would need to submit a special report and take specific measures." So what Mr. Zupljanin is suggesting, the collegium accepts those discussions and responsibility for carrying it out. I would now like you to go back to page 5 in the B/C/S, in the Serbian version, and that is page 8 in the English version. The part that the Prosecutor showed you says that the army and the Crisis Staff or the War Presidency demand that as many Muslims as possible be assembled, and it talks about these camps and the conditions in these camps. utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Then after that, let's go back to page 26 again. utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krulj, this is precisely the way to deal with problems if some illegal matters crop up, and that is the way that Mr. Zupljanin dealt with it. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He followed the procedure where you would inform the minister and the relevant bodies, which would be followed by appropriate action. utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And this is the same thing that you would do had you had the same sort of problems?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In this specific case, Zupljanin was pointed to the problem of the collection centres under whose authority they were, the problems that were cropping up, and he wanted instructions and assistance in order to resolve that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could the witness now be shown 1D55, please. The document was shown to you by my colleague Mr. Zecevic this morning, and now I would like you just to look at paragraph 2 where it says: "The security of collection centres shall be the direct responsibility of the Serbian Army ..." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And so this dispatch is the result of the initiative started by Mr. Zupljanin at that meeting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could we now go back to Exhibit P160, please. Mr. Krulj, let's look at page 5. According to these minutes, Mr. Zupljanin says: "The financing of the MUP and the services is done by the SAO Krajina government. When the financing is resolved, we will have fewer interventions and less influence." As far as I understood you from this discussion, practically local authorities in the municipality financed the police for a certain period of time because there were no communications.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And they also tried to exert their influence on the local organs of command, trying to influence their work.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And this is the problem pointed out by Zupljanin. Now I'm going to go back to the conclusions. Page 28, item 16. The ministry -- well, let me allow you to find it first.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
