utterances.text: "The Ministry of the Interior must be financed exclusively from the budget of the Serb republic." Do you see that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So Stojan Zupljanin's initiative adopted in these conclusions, and as a result of that certain people were entrusted with the execution of that task. We can see that from here. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now we're going back to page 5 again. I'm sorry that I have to do it this way, but I have -- my intention is to show clearly what actually Stojan Zupljanin said and what the conclusions were and how things developed after that. So can you please look at this part where he says that the functional network of -- of connections was shattered. Connections were not functioning. So the same thing applied in the territory of your own municipality; is that correct? The communications were not functioning?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the next page. This is page 6 now.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zupljanin says here exactly what you were talking about today, and that is that the military judicial system was not functioning, that judges had not been elected, and that overlapping jurisdictions or mutual jurisdictions would need to be regulated.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And then he goes on to say that there are no judges for the criminal cases. They're afraid, they're exposed to threats in some municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Could you please repeat your previous answer when I was asking you about the court jurisdictions. You said yes. I heard you say that, but it was not recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yes, that was a major problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And then there is this second conclusion here that several thousand court cases are not completed. There aren't enough judges for criminal cases. Judges are afraid. They are exposed to threats, and hardcore criminals were being released from prison, which made it difficult for the rule of law to function as well as for the work of the police organs. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So this was the same problem that you were encountering in your municipality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Also, Mr. Zupljanin goes on to say about measures being taken that would need to be taken for -- some unclear matters would need to be resolved, that you would need to resolve the status of criminal case judges, and resolve some other problems there that affected the work of the MUP. All of that is stated here, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: After that, I'm going back to page 26 again.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Where it says in one of the conclusions that the work of the military judicial organs, and they're functioning. Then we have page 27, paragraph 14: For the purposes of resolving existing problems and outstanding issues it is necessary to organise a joint meeting with the Ministry of Justice at which the following problems would also be discussed. In essence, the bulk of these proposals and failings were included in the minutes of that meeting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to go to page 29 now. That is the last page. The last paragraph where it says: "The summary of this meeting with the conclusions should be submitted to the CSBs for further direction and better quality work and also to the prime minister and the president of the Presidency for their information and for the purpose of taking further measures to improve the work of the Ministry of the Interior." So we can conclude on the basis of that that this -- these conclusions and the minutes were also submitted to the government and to the Presidency and not only to the CSBs so that these matters could be dealt with adequately.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So specifically in relation to what Stojan Zupljanin said and his request for assistance in relation to these matters, he practically fulfilled his obligations pursuant to the regulations of the work of the MUP and his authority and powers by informing those authorised and by seeking that certain steps be taken.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Just as you would have done in an identical situation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I just have one part here that Mr. Zupljanin spoke about, but this is then included in the conclusions, so it's not really subject for analysis. So in relation to this part I'm not going to put any more questions to you. I did have one question that had nothing directly to do with this meeting. When Mr. Zecevic showed you these rules about disciplinary responsibilities applied during imminent danger of war and the state of war he - actually these rules date from September 1992 - according to those regulations and prior regulations initiating disciplinary proceedings for MUP employees is something that is the responsibility of the commander or the chief of the public security station. The initiation of such proceedings should he find out about certain violations.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The disciplinary proceedings are initiated by any employee. That is their right. The proposal to initiate proceedings is something else. That is submitted by the authorised superior officer of the station or the centre to a commission or to the Prosecutor. Here we're talking about summary proceedings, and I think there is no need for me to go into that, but that is the way how a disciplinary proceedings are initiated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no more further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Krulj, I want to go over some of the matters you've been asked about by the Defence in the last couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. Korner. Do you need the lectern?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, no, I'm fine, thanks. I've got one down there somewhere. I'll live without it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, first of all, you were asked a number of questions by Mr. Zecevic in relation to how you dealt with paramilitary formation that came into your municipality. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just get this right. First of all, yours, as we saw at the beginning, was a small municipality with a very, very small proportion of Muslims. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was there much difference between the size of your municipality, Ljubinje, and those of Bileca and Gacko?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In what sense? Were they much bigger?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Much bigger, with much more population. Bileca about 12.000 inhabitants, and Gacko perhaps even more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And each of those, as we've seen, had SJBs. Gacko and Bileca.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can I just confirm, because I'm going to show you a document a bit later, but the head of the SJB in Bileca was Mr. Goran Vojovic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Goran Vujovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Vujovic. So sorry. And was the commander a man named Miroslav Duka?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in Gacko, is that right, it was a gentleman named Popovic who was the head of the SJB?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm not sure whether it was so at the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, as I understand what you're saying, the only information you received about events in either Gacko or Bileca was at meetings that were held at Trebinje with the other chiefs of the SJBs?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Or obviously collegiums.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At internal collegiums those matters were not discussed, and you could see it based on the documents that you have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Particularly on the diary.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And you told, I think it was either Mr. Zecevic or Mr. Krgovic, a few minutes ago that you only heard about what was happening in Bileca and prisoners privately. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly through private channels, and that was before the meeting that was held in Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want to come back to that aspect a little later. You've also been shown a large number of documents emanating largely from Mico Stanisic by Mr. Zecevic, and do I understand this correctly, that you are able to recall that you received each and every one of these documents?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not able to remember now, but if I take a look at the document and I can see to whom it was addressed, then I can remember that it reached us. I can guarantee you that it reached every public security station. Now, if you were to tell me, "Give me a quote from a document of the 26th of June, 1992," then I wouldn't be able to do that, but if I see a document like I saw it here today, then I can claim with certainty that that document reached my public security station.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, but -- you see, this is quite important, and nobody blames you for this, Mr. Krulj. Are you saying it's simply because it's addressed to the SJB or the CSB you must have received it or that you can actually recall receiving it, because there's a difference.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember receiving these documents. And there were a lot of documents with similar content.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So even if you didn't have to take any particular action in your own municipality, you can still remember that you received those documents?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And so there was no problem in getting those documents to you. Communication certainly worked to that extent?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we reached it after ten or -- perhaps we received it after 10 or 15 days via courier. It certainly didn't reach us on the day the document was written.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But -- that's why I wanted to confirm. You're quite sure you got all these documents.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And you can verify that in the archives of our station.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to talk to you a little bit, please -- or I want to ask you - sorry, I don't know exactly what I corrected somebody else for - about something that you said in respect of a document, which I believe has now been numbered 1D46. And if we could have that on the screen. This is this order of the 15th of May dealing with the wartime organisation of the ministry, and you were shown item 8. Please, in English and in Serbian. And 9, which is the setting up of the disciplinary matters and the setting up of this staff. And you told us that violation of regulations and failure to carry out tasks which had been ordered in an appropriate display of disciplinary and criminal punishment, et cetera. You were asked was that abided by in practice and you said yes. How do you know that? How do you know it was abided by in practice?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When talking about this, I speak of the institution where I worked, and I can state with full responsibility that I upheld, I abided by this order. And as for you mean how it went in practice, I can explain. For example, if somebody committed such and such crime, then, yes, sanctions followed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. No. Sorry --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In accordance with the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is what I'm trying to get at. You can say that in your municipality you abided by it, but do you have any idea whether everybody else abided by it? That's the question.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave responses in relation to my municipality, and that's how I understood the questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly, Mr. Krulj. It's not your fault, but the impression may have been given that you were giving an answer for everywhere else in the whole Trebinje section. And then you -- it went on, the question, item 9 said that: "A staff should be established, and this staff is being established only in the structural sense, so to speak," said Mr. Zecevic, page 35, and not in the sense of effective command and control; isn't that right?" And you said, "Well, I never received any kind of letter signed by a staff commander so you are right. "Did you ever receive any sort of official letter from the police staff in 1992? Do you have any information indicating that the CSB you belonged to ever received a sort of letter sent by staff or staff commander?" And you said: "No, I don't know that anybody received it." Right. Can I ask you to have a look now, please, at 65 ter 2369. It will come up on the screen in front of you. Eventually. Now, this is a decision by Mico Stanisic, dated -- I'm not sure what it's dated, but it says "Following the 15th of May." Decision to appoint Krsto Savic to the position of chief of Trebinje CSB security services centre, member of the Serbian republic of the interior staff for command and control of the overall forces of the Ministry of the Interior. And then pursuant to the powers, statement of reasons, et cetera, establishing a staff for command and control of the ministry's forces in accordance with position held, et cetera. So were you -- are you saying to the Court you didn't know that in fact Krsto Savic had also been appointed chief of this staff, or appointed to the staff?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is being appointed to a member of the staff as chief of CSB. So he had previously been appointed chief of CSB and then staff member. As I have said yesterday, I didn't see this decision, and I also said that I didn't see the signature right here at the bottom where it says "Minister." I never saw somebody sign as Chief of Staff. And as for Krsto being a staff member, yes, I could see it on the basis of the previous document where it said who the staff consisted of. It says who was the chief, who was deputy assistant, and then all chiefs of CSBs, and Krsto was a chief of a CSB. So based from that document I could see that he was a member of the staff, and as for the decision actually appointing him, no, I never saw that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. At the moment I'm just asking you whether you knew that in fact such a staff did exist and that Krsto Savic was a member of it.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I could see it from the document that we saw before this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. But did you know in 1992, in May, that this staff existed and that Krsto Savic was a member of it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, in those circumstances, may I ask this be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have no objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P170.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I just want to ask you a little bit more about this business of the resubordination that you were asked about of police to the army. You told us - I'm just going to find the place - that you had a conversation -- sorry. I'm just trying to find my ... yes. Yeah. This was at page 46 of the -- the -- yesterday's LiveNote. That the brigade commander asked you to provide assistance to him with policemen, and you said: "I didn't have to be pushed to do this because certain areas had to be closed off. I attended the meeting, and I accepted to give some of my men to resubordinate them." Do you remember saying that? Do we take it from that, when you say you accepted, that you had a choice as to whether or not you were to supply reserve police for the purposes of the army?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did have a choice in accordance with the agreement with the senior officials at the centre, especially if there was no communication. And if I didn't make a decision within ten minutes, then it would have been too late if they informed me three days later. So I could have not sent a unit. Because if I were to wait for somebody to actually send me an official request and then for me to officially respond, then it could have been too late. So, yes, I was authorised to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no. I understand that. I just -- so it's not that the brigade commander could order you to supply them, he could request, and you could decide whether yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. He could not order me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just understand this: Supposing when one of your policemen was engaged under the command of the military in an action he had committed a criminal offence such as looting, who would be responsible for initiating the prosecution against the -- or the investigation, rather, not the prosecution, against this individual?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time while he is resubordinated -- it was never just one single person. It was mostly a unit at the level of a platoon, say 20 people. So during that period of time, it is the military resubordination that is responsible and competent. Now, if that unit were to be sent back to the MUP forces, and that's precisely for that reason that we sent the command of the unit as well, then there would be disciplinary proceedings, because the documents say if somebody does or has done previously a crime, then, yes, we could send the information and the report, but it would be the military hierarchy that would actually have the jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But as you say if -- I just want -- so we can get this clear. If the platoon came back to resume normal police duties and there was a report that someone had committed a crime whilst on the military duties, you would be responsible -- I say "you," but the police would be responsible for beginning the investigation.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the commander of the battalion who was duty-bound to start the investigation or, rather, military police and the security. Each brigade had a military police detachment and a security department, and they were stronger than a police station in Ljubinje. And each town had a brigade with military police and military security. If they were to fail to do that, then upon their return we would submit a criminal report and take disciplinary action to expel the perpetrator due to a crime that had been committed earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. You say to expel you would submit a criminal report to whom, the military prosecutor or to the ordinary prosecutor, the civil prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: After their return, then it was us who were duty-bound to submit it to civilian prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. And just while we're on that topic, if a crime was reported to you and you made investigations, even if the investigations showed that the perpetrator was likely to have been a member of the military at the time, would you submit a report still to the civilian prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to reply to that. If he was a member of the military, then normally it would be military police who would come and take over that case from us with all the appropriate documents that we had about the crime, the act, and so on, and they would submit it to the military prosecutor in Bileca. They would submit a report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we just -- sorry, let's look at an actual example from your own municipality. You told us about the mosque being blown up, and you told us you carried out an inquiry -- or an investigation. Do you remember telling us that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Supposing your investigations which you had begun had shown that it was likely to have been a military unit that blew up the mosque, would you then submit a report to the civilian prosecutor or simply contact the -- the military police?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was -- if it was a military unit, we would get in touch with the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you wouldn't submit any kind of report to the prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could submit a report, the basic report, to the civilian prosecutor, but if it was a military unit, then it was -- then it is the military prosecutor who has jurisdiction. Had we uncovered who the perpetrator was, then the civilian prosecutor would declare himself not to be competent and would send the case over to the military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. This is what I'm trying to get at. It was actually the civilian prosecutor, wasn't it, not the police who made the decision which of them -- two of them had jurisdiction. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, can I move --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, it's 12 -- it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We'll resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Krulj, I want to go over some of the things you said again about the Special Police. You told Mr. Zecevic at - here we are - page 48 of yesterday's transcript, who was going over what you said to me in chief, about the special unit that was established by the SAO Herzegovina, which was sent to the Dubrovnik front. Right.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Specijalna, not Posebna unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I fully understand.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I fully understand the distinction you're making, but I just wanted to concentrate on this unit. You told Mr. Zecevic it was not under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of the Interior, it did not carry out any police tasks but only participated in combat. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how did you know that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that as a member of the MUP, that nobody in the territory of the Trebinje centre had any sort of jurisdiction or competence over that unit. I said that that unit didn't come to my territory, but I also know that commander in Trebinje or chief on Bileca could not deploy that unit either, nor could anybody else among us do that. And I can tell you that the centre had not yet been established when the unit was set up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- that's what you're telling us, but I want to come back to that in a moment. How do you know - or are you saying this is what you were told by somebody else - that this unit carried out combat activities?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: From talking to my colleagues in Trebinje, I knew that they went to the area of Ravno and area of Mostar. That's all I learned from the conversation. I never saw that unit taking charge of traffic or patrolling in town or conducting any sort of checks. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no. But you wouldn't expect a special unit to do traffic duties, would you? A special unit was designed, as you told us, to deal with outbreaks of public disorder, roadblocks and things like that, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are Posebna units what you're talking about, about disturbances of law and order and other things. That's done by Posebna units. As for Specijalna units it was a combat unit of SAO Herzegovina that had nothing to do with public security stations in the territory of Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So you're quite clear on that. So Mico Stanisic as minister of the interior had nothing whatsoever to do with this particular unit that you're talking about. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time he didn't. On the 28th of March I was in Mostar at the security centre there having coffee with my colleagues and Specijalna Jedinica was already in existence at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And this is the unit that you say contained criminals, but also, as you said when you gave evidence when I was asking you questions, two members of the regular police.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said two.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were several members of police who had left police force and were members of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But you said -- sorry, the word you used was "active policemen."

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, who used to be active policemen and then they left police force and joined that unit. They were active policemen who had left police force and went to the army on their own initiative.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, this isn't the army we're talking about. I'm now talking -- leave this -- I'm talking about this group called the Special Police set up by the SAO Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that these people earlier used to be active policemen, and then they transferred to that unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But in order to transfer to that unit, they must have got permission, must they not, from their superiors in the police force?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They simply left their job as policemen and then moved on to the other unit, and by doing so they were taken off any duties at the police. If somebody failed to come to work without legitimate excuse for more than three days, that would constitute a grave violation of discipline and automatically would terminate them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can I ask you how you know that that's what happened to these several members of the police? How do you know that they left without permission?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know these people. I don't know these members. I am talking about what I heard. I don't know people who were in that unit. I said that from Ljubinje, from my station, there were no men who joined that unit, but I think that that was the standard procedure of the Ministry of the Interior, regular procedure. I have to say that at the time we received our salaries from the centre in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Did you also hear that the men who were in these -- in this particular SAO unit committed crimes?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear of any crimes, but I did hear that they behaved inappropriately, drank, broke things, grabbed drinks in certain areas around Mostar, and that they also seized materiel and equipment, especially vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You see, you told Mr. Zecevic earlier that one of the things you wanted to do in coming here was to protect the reputation and work of members of the police who did their job honourably. Is that something you feel quite strongly about?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you really want me to say, I mean, it's for the purposes of protection of the truth and the dignity of those people and the people who honourably and professionally conducted their duties. Not everything should be placed on the shoulders of the police. The police didn't have an easy time during the time of this dirty war, and you probably don't have an idea about that. If I were -- if I were to tell you one particular instance that had to do with me when I was in a vehicle and ten people were firing at this vehicle where I was in, and this was something that was under the jurisdiction of the military, and then those perpetrators, the following day, were actually released to go home. They were allowed to -- they were relieved temporarily to go on holiday. That's the story.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Krulj, can I say I'm not suggesting that you acted dishonourably. I'm just -- I just want to look at some of the things that you've said, that's all. I'd like you to have a look, please, at an article that was published in "Glas" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think there is a misunderstanding, clarification is perhaps needed for me eventually. You're insisting about the active policemen that were in those Special Police Unit. I think you were referring to the Specijalna unit, weren't you? THE PROSECUTOR: I'm referring to the unit that he's described that was set up by the SAO Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's the Specijalna. But I checked it on the transcript yesterday, and I think that the active policemen that the witness meant were in the other unit, the Posebna.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's what he told us yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. What he said on -- and he's just confirmed it. What he said on -- on the -- whatever date it was -- the 26th, Monday, at page 2001, 2002: "There was one unit called the Special Police, but this was not under the jurisdiction of the CSB because the CSB had not been formed yet. This was formed by the government of the SAO Herzegovina, and there were a couple of people," and he now says, "who were active policemen."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But yesterday, and I'm referring to page 53, line 9 and 10, I specifically asked whether it was Specijalna or -- what's the other name? Posebna. And there I got the answer Posebna. So perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He's talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We need to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you go back to you -- this, he was talking about a different -- he was talking about the PJP, which was different from this unit. That's what he was talking about. All right. Shall we -- I accept it probably needs clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we just understand this. In the group that -- the group you've called Special Police set up by the SAO Herzegovina, did that contain people who you now say were active police but left and transferred to this unit?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear of such cases, yes, but may I clarify one thing, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 1st of April, 1992, we belonged to the Mostar centre. There was no security centre in Trebinje. The chief of the centre in Mostar was a Croat, Slobodan Bozic. He was my boss. Do you believe that that Specijalna Jedinica unit was part of the police and the centre in Mostar because there was no security centre in Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. At the moment what I'm trying to concentrate on is this group that you say was set up by the SAO Herzegovina that has no connection with the -- the formal MUP of the Ministry of the Interior. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was a paramilitary formation that named itself Specijalna Jedinica Policija special unit of the police, or it was named that by somebody from the leadership of the SAO Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I think maybe we can clarify this because you've mentioned the 1st of April and it's obvious an important date.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we have a look please at 65 ter 10142. No, that's not it. 10142. I don't know what's up on ... And I think we need to -- no, that's fine. Yes. That will do. Slightly to the left in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I put my colleague Ms. Korner on notice that I would in principle object to admission of -- of these documents. So let me just briefly explain. Your Honours, the theory of the Prosecution is that the media in 1991 and 1992 were used as a propaganda machinery for -- from all sides in Bosnia. Therefore, they are alleging that this -- this media was creating a sense of fear, was building up the war effort or hatred towards other -- other nationalities, ethnicities, and so on and so on. Now, if that is -- if that is the situation, which we -- which I personally believe is true, then I don't think that it is consistent with that position that the -- that the Prosecution uses the very same propaganda documents establishing quite the contrary situation. I'm not saying -- I'm just using this opportunity because this is the first time that we are having a media article presented in our case to state this as a general objection that we have towards admission of the media -- media articles. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's an overstatement of our position. When I opened the case, I drew your attention to certain organs such as the Informator in Sanski Most which I said was certainly propaganda, but media articles where, you know, report, and indeed when it comes to Banja Luka, we'll be putting in the whole of the -- the "Glas" articles about the SOS. Media articles are admissible in this Tribunal with all the caveats, and I think we've discussed this before. We're not saying that all the media all of the time was an instrument of propaganda for the SDS or the SDA or whichever party it was. We're saying in some cases, particularly the publications where the language used is inflammatory, that's one thing. This article is a straightforward report, apparently, and I simply want to ask the witness about what's contained in that report in the light of what he said. And it's the same with many other articles as I say that we'll be introducing and which have been entered into evidence on many occasions before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, do I also understand your objection also to be to the question that she's about to put to him about the article apart from the question of admissibility, and the question of admissibility, I would have thought that what Mrs. Korner has said is the answer to the question, but did I understand your objection to be even to putting the question to him that she will --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, not at all, Your Honours. I just in principle wanted to object because this is the first time we're going to have this article, and I want the record to clearly show that we are taking in principle the objection to admission of media articles in this case. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, there's nothing like rewriting the jurisprudence in the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. This is an article that you were -- you were familiar, were you, with the "Glas" newspaper, Mr. Krulj?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear of it, but I don't read the paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But this reports apparently on the 1st of April that: "The SAO Herzegovina police and Special Police Units were established in Trebinje today. Following the national anthem and the inspection of the units, the policemen took their solemn oath. "Mico Stanisic, minister the interior of the Serbian republic stressed at this celebration that the people of the Serbian republic have their own Ministry of the Interior," and so on and so forth. Now, firstly, were you present at this parade or whatever it was, ceremony?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was in civilian clothing, and I was expecting a meeting, but I will tell you that on the 28th, after the cistern exploded in Mostar, all the Serbs ran away from Mostar, all the civilians, the judges, all those who managed to escape from the -- to the eastern part, and then the policemen who came from Mostar came to Trebinje. So this is not a review of any kind of Special Police because if it says so in the paper it's a pure lie, because it's a matter of some 20-odd active policemen, exclusively active service policemen. And I wasn't there in that review line in front of the centre where those people were standing when the minister arrived, but I was standing next to that line, and I was in civilian clothing, and they do not -- there was no mention of anything like that. If that is what is said here, I do not accept that, that it was any kind of special unit. It was just regular active-duty members of the police force, and the reason for that was the one that I explained before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, first of all, you said that -- okay. The newspaper reporter has got it completely wrong. There were no Special Police at this parade. Can you just say -- is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I state that with full responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, do you know why Mico Stanisic was there reviewing just 20-odd active policemen?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krsto Savic was the one who did the review, while Mico Stanisic came to inform us about the new Law on Internal Affairs and about the beginning of the functioning of the new security centre in Trebinje. That meeting we held very briefly in the premises of the public security station in Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. You -- exactly. You told us about the meeting, but -- sorry. I'm just going back to the document for a moment. So the words "SAO Herzegovina police" and "Special Police Unit" you say simply aren't right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the presence in front of the station, there was no Specijalna Policija from SAO Herzegovina there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. On the face of this article, the -- what you've just told us about the SAO Special Police would be wrong, that's right, isn't it? What you told us earlier about it being the police, it had nothing to do with the Ministry of the Interior. It would be wrong, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true there was a police that had nothing to do with the Ministry of Internal Affairs, and those police members were not at this review on this particular day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I'm not seeking to put this in at the moment without further [indiscernible], but could I have it marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: My objection still stands, and I believe the witness directly gave the reason why I was objecting, that it contains not -- not truthful -- it's a document which is not truthful at all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's a matter for Your Honours to decide rather than Mr. Zecevic. Your Honours have heard what the witness said, and you've seen what the article said. At the moment I'm not asking for it to be admitted as an exhibit. I'm simply asking for it to be marked for identification. Whether it's untrue or not, I heard what the witness said. Your Honours decide whether or not you accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, I agree with Ms. Korner. It is just that the witness was there, and he confirms that there was no -- there was nothing like -- like this parade of SAO Special Police, and that is exactly the right example of the propaganda which I was talking about. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I -- I'm sorry, it isn't propaganda. It's a report. What's propaganda about it? It's simply a report. But could I ask just one further question, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I ask one further question and then we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Are you saying that there was no Special Police Unit as well that was set up in Trebinje at this time, 1st of April?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were active police officers who were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know. I understand what you said about who was at the parade. I'm simply asking you whether -- are you saying as well there was not the establishment at this period of a Special Police Unit, and by that I mean which comes under the minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was formed and it existed permanently pursuant to provisions of the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. So there was -- you see, we're going around in circles now. There was a Special Police Unit set up in Trebinje around this period. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but this review was not a review of that unit. One vehicle filled with policemen came from each municipality accompanying the leadership that had come to attend the meeting, and these were just regular active police officers who in front of the police station were lined up by Krsto Savic in honour of the arrival of the minister of the interior. It was not a formation of the Posebna Jedinica unit. There was summons to come on the 1st of April, and so there was maximum of five policemen per vehicle, and so the review actually was a review of regular active-duty police forces. This is not the only such heading. This was -- there are many such headings, headlines. It was written by the Serbian press. They were writing how the unit was armed and so on. There was all kinds of things that were being written at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Tell me something. Is there a film in existence of this parade that you've ever seen?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't, but perhaps it does exist. It's possible that there was a recording, taping of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally on this -- this document, did Mico Stanisic say words to the effect of, "Our legality and legitimacy are derived from the legitimate will of the Serbian and other peoples expressed at the plebescite and declared their wish for their own Assembly, their own constitution and their own laws"? Did he say something like that at this ceremony?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he did, and I think that he had a full right to say that. What you just referred to did occur over the previous month, the plebiscite, the formation of the Assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and mostly Mr. Stanisic asked that the police continued to work the way it worked before pursuant to the regulations in effect. There was no insightful language or anything like that, although it's quite a different matter how this was portrayed in the press.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, in that event, partially accepted. May I just have it marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 171 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, the -- sorry. Yes. All right. Do you agree that there was in fact set up at the CSB in Trebinje a Special Police Unit, what you call the PJP?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a unit of the police that was called Posebna Jedinica Policija, the PJP at the Trebinje station. It was not called Specijalna Jedinica Policija, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, can you have a look, please, at a document, 65 ter 155.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We're going to make it -- enlarge it, if that's what you said. I didn't get a translation. Now, can you just read out, please, the Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We have been made aware of the situation and the problems --"

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, sorry. I'm so sorry. Mr. Krulj, not that. The top, because it's been translated in English as something.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: "CSB security services centre Trebinje. "To the Special Police Brigade Detachment Commander."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So to the commander of the Specijalna police. "We have been aware of the situation and problems of the Trebinje police detachment. It is imperative that as soon as possible --"

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Stop. This says -- do we agree it has been translated both orally and in writing as "Special Police"? So that's what it was called at Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Detachment of the special brigade of the police of Trebinje, and the special brigade of the police is at the seat of the ministry. Here this is addressed to the commander of the detachment of the Special Police Brigade, and that was Karisik Milenko and the assistant of -- actually, it was signed by the Assistant Minister, Tomislav Kovac. Can you please just tell me what the date of the document is if you --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Regrettably we can't.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Regrettably it doesn't have a date on it. It's 251 of the -- but can I just ask you this: "We have been made aware of a situation, problems of the Trebinje police detachment." In your view this is the detachment from the Special Brigade under Karisik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is late 1992 and early 1993. Well, this is all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, yes. That's the next thing I want to ask you about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think I'll have that made an exhibit at the moment. Could I have it marked for identification because I think we need to investigate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't have a problem. I just want to remind my learned colleague that this document was withdrawn from your 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, that's news --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is the information that I received from my assistant.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, if it was withdrawn it's news to us, but as I said, Your Honour, I'm not seeking to have it admitted as an exhibit but obviously just marked for identification at the moment. I think we need to make a bit more inquiries about it. Can we just check though?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: If it is not on the 65 ter list, it is inadmissible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, no, Your Honour. We've been through this I thought. We've been marking them for identification a number of documents which aren't on our 65 ter list on the basis that we would apply to amend our 65 ter list. If we don't get it marked for identification it's a bit difficult to bring it back up again. So can we have that marked for identification? And apparently it's on our 65 ter list still.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It wasn't any objection. I was just notified that it was withdrawn. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So it's marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P172 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Just very simply, are you saying Milenko Karisik was only appointed in charge of Special Police in the end of 1992 and early 1993?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was appointed earlier, but I think that the detachment of the brigade in Trebinje was formed at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this is a legal document that is in keeping with the regulations. The only thing is that it is not dated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. That's fine. So I didn't want to -- I didn't want to show you earlier documents. Milenko Karisik was in fact appointed, wasn't he, early on in 1992 to head the -- the Ministry of the Interior Special Police Brigade, and then when the CSB ones were abolished later, there was a new -- there was a formation of a new brigade towards the end of 1992. Is that what you're saying? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know. As far as I know, from the 4th of April there was the special brigade of the police under the command of Karisik. And as for CSBs, abolishing it, I don't know. Maybe somebody from the ministry knows about it. I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, don't worry, I'm not going to trouble you with it. All right, that's all I want to ask you, please, about the Special Police. Well, actually, no, there's one other document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I have 65 ter 2132 just to finally put an end to this. We've only translated, Your Honours, the top bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you agree that this appears to be a list of employees of the special unit for the the payment of salaries for the month of April 1992, for the SJB in Bileca? And do you recognise any of the names on the list?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recognise a single policeman here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. We'll have to deal with that some other way, Your Honours. And that can come down.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Leaving the Special Police, please. I want to deal now with this matter of this particular order from Mico Stanisic that you were shown yesterday and today, or the series of orders, 23, 24, and 26 of July. Do I understand what you're saying to be this: that police officers who were thought to have committed criminal offences would be dismissed from the police and sent to the army because that was automatic, that if they left the police they would go into the army? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that measures of disciplinary and criminal responsibility were taken against them, and in addition to that, their names and their files were sent to the Ministry of Defence in order for them to be enlisted into the army units.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's just have a look at the first one that you -- you looked at yesterday. I have no idea what the P number is. It was 1 Defence 2751. I thought -- yes. I don't know what the P number was, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well -- it's a Defence document, yes. That's what I just said, 2751.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you told Mr. Zecevic you definitely received this document. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it's repeating the -- or they're forwarding to you the dispatch of the 23rd of July, with the order that "all members of the MUP who have committed crimes," and we've got that one, "prior to or since the start of combat take legal measures to remove them from our ranks, relieve them of duty, and put them at the disposal of the army of the Serbian republic." Now, on the face of that that does not mention, does it, anywhere, taking criminal proceedings against them. It simply says, get rid of them from the police and stick them in the army, to put it colloquially, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you want to relieve somebody of duty, if you want to remove them from the police, how are you going to prove that that person committed a crime if there hadn't been any criminal reports? And there were such cases where people had criminal reports filed against them, not traffic violations, and they were still members of police. And here they're ordering that anybody who was subject to criminal proceedings or there were criminal reports filed against them, that they need to be removed from the ranks of police, because how can you dismiss somebody if you don't have evidence that that person committed a crime? You need to have evidence, and that is criminal report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But hang on. But nowhere does it say, does it, in that record, and we look at the original order itself, or we can, which came out on the 23rd of July, it doesn't mention the word or criminal proceedings had been taken, does it? So if you read the document on the face of it, it just says if they've committed crimes, remove them and send them to the army. And I appreciate what you say.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The law is what prescribes what a crime is, and no order is needed in relation to each single crime. What they need to do is file a criminal report in case somebody committed a crime. And in cases where a criminal report was filed, three, five, or I don't know how many months ago, then we were duty-bound to relieve that person of police duties. I don't think that they should have written, "If somebody commits a crime, make sure that you file a criminal report." I don't think there's a need to specify it so plainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. We'll come on to this, what's further down in this document in a moment, but are you saying that -- well, first -- no. The first question is: Why was it necessary, if it was already legally in place, for such an order to be issued in the first place if the law already said that police officers who committed crimes against whom a criminal report has been filed should be suspended from duty? Why was that necessary?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because there had been such cases in certain stations, and because ministry had learned that there were such cases in certain SJBs and that people who had committed crimes were still in the ranks of police, and I think that this is fully clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is it your understanding of this order that as His Honour Judge Harhoff asked you, if you had a police officer in custody who had, for example, killed a prisoner who was in his custody, or raped a woman who was in his custody, that instead of the criminal proceedings continuing, he would be released and sent to the army? Is that what your understanding is, Mr. Krulj? You say you've got this order.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could I understand it in that way? I'm explaining it for the hundredth time. That would be equal to pardoning somebody from criminal prosecution. How could police do something like that? Where did you come up with such a thesis? So if somebody goes and kills somebody and as a punishment is sent to the army? It is simply beyond me to think that somebody could legitimately believe that that was possible. If somebody killed somebody, then they cannot go to the army. And if they were awaiting trial, then they would go to the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But on the face of this order, where is the distinction drawn, Mr. Krulj, between an offence which allows you to suspend the prosecution and send him to the army and one which does not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I disagree.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no. I'm asking you. I'm asking you the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you don't mind, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Where in this order which you say you received can one see, reading the order, a distinction between the sort of crimes that allow you to suspend criminal proceedings and the sort of crimes which do not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have to object, because --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will reply --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that there is any basis for -- for this question, I think, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The witness -- the witness answered, and I wouldn't like to answer -- to give me reasons, because I wouldn't like to influence the witness, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: What I -- thank you, Mr. Zecevic. What I was going to ask Ms. Korner was having regard to the witness's answer which you may or may not accept, is the -- in fairness to -- to the witness, aren't you inviting an argument in respect of this document of which he was not the author?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no. I'm going to come on to it -- [indiscernible] deal with another part of this document, but I'm asking him as a recipient how would he have known from this order if he'd had somebody in custody who had allegedly committed a murder and someone in custody who had allegedly stolen from a house, how he would distinguish between those who could be sent to the army and those who could not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: As a recipient?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As a recipient. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you understand the question, Mr. Krulj? Supposing you had somebody who allegedly had committed a murder, beaten a prisoner to death, and someone who had stolen from a house, how would you distinguish which one remained in custody based on this order, and which one -- the criminal proceedings continued against and which was released?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood your question. This document means that members of the police are educated enough so that when a crime is committed, for each crime they need to file a criminal report. In addition to a criminal report, that member would be removed from police duties. If that person committed a crime, he would be put in detention for up to three days. Prosecutor and the relevant court would be informed of it. I suppose in that case the Court would extend the pre-trial detention. The investigative judge would have done it as it was regulated at the time, and that person would have been in gaol during that period of time. Whereas with respect to the person who stole something, a criminal report would be filed for theft, for having committed theft. That would have been sent to the prosecutor's office. And while awaiting trial, that person would have been placed at the disposal of the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were our regulations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's -- I hear what you say on this. Let's go down to the end of this particular order. Dispatch -- it repeats what it says is in dispatch of the 23rd of July and then dispatch number 0211 of the 24th of July. This is where we get the mention apparently of the proceedings. "It is necessary that all members of the MUP who have been held criminally accountable or against whom criminal proceedings are under way in the competent courts be relieved of duty and be put at the disposal of the army of the Serbian republic." Exactly. Right. Now, I would like you to have a look, please, as you were shown this morning, of the 24th of July dispatch number 0211, which was produced as an exhibit. If it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honours, I have the objection. I believe the witness answered many times, and this is getting nowhere. He -- he answered that this was prescribed by the law, and that is the basis on what they were doing. He said that --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's a --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He said that five teams at.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's a completely different point, Mr. Zecevic, if you wait a moment. I'm not pursuing what he says about this now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Can we find, I think it was 65 ter but it was produced as a Defence exhibit 18 -- 188. It's 1D59, the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. This is allegedly, this is the order 20211 signed on behalf of Mico Stanisic, which is allegedly referred to in that 26th of April one from Krsto Savic.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now -- yes, I see. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in fact -- don't worry. This is not a point I want to proceed with. In fact, Your Honour, there's no further point I want to make on these documents then. I made a mistake in my -- no.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we finally then, please -- that's all I'm going to ask you on this topic. You were shown the document -- no. You were asked by Mr. Krgovic -- sorry, there's one last point, not on this document. War crimes. You were asked by, I think, Mr. Zecevic about investigation of crimes, and in particular, war crimes, and about the difficulties with that. I want you to have a look, please, at -- it's gone again. Yes. Document 65 ter 127. This is an order from Mico Stanisic, dated the 16th of May, to the security centres in -- including Trebinje. And can we go, please, to the third page in English and the second page in B/C/S. "War crimes. "Measures and activities conducted to document war crimes. These activities must involve collection of information and documents on war crimes against the Serbs." Did you get this order?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Since only preliminary information was collected at the police stations and war crimes were processed by CSB at the seat, and it was mostly done by crime prevention police. So perhaps a letter was sent based on this document to the SJB.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So, what, you saw every other order from Mico Stanisic but never got sent this one?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that I saw this one too. I'm familiar with the content and I have said so. Either it was copied from something else. Every order that was sent to public security stations to everybody and to CSBs, to everybody, was something that I received as well, whereas an order that was sent only to centres, security centres, was sometimes was forwarded to public security stations in its original form or it could have been copied into a different form and sent to public security stations. This is the usual way the police conducts communication.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. But you are familiar with the -- with this instruction to collect material and investigate war crimes against Serbs? Do you ever recall receiving an order --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- from Mico Stanisic which said conduct investigations into war crimes generally, whoever they may have been committed against?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that can be seen partially in this order and can also be seen in the form that was attached, the form that required that entries be made about the ethnicity and religion, and that was the form that accompanied this order.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This order of May?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The form?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Because you were shown a form of -- for a later document, much, much later, dealing with the investigations into camps, which I'm going to come on to. Did you ever -- did you ever conduct an investigation on the orders of Mico Stanisic or on Krsto Savic in relation to any offences committed against Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not pursuant to an order. However, there were some crimes, property crimes, in my municipality, some minor crimes, and we did it based on the law, not pursuant to an order.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And this is the final topic I want to -- you were asked about Bileca by, I believe, Mr. Zecevic or Mr. Krgovic, and you were shown a document, 2765. I think it was. Sorry, 2764. Sorry. You were asked about collection centres. If you look at that. I have no idea what the number was. D35 -- 55. 10th of August. Were you aware at all, Mr. Krulj, that there had been publication of -- in international media of camps, particularly in the Prijedor area?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were you aware that as a result of that this is why this -- there was this hive of activity about prisons and collection centres within the Serbian republic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, were you aware that these letters asking about -- and orders in respect of collection centres and prisons came about as a result of the international publicity? If you weren't aware, say so.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were asked by I think again His Honour Judge Harhoff, the difference between a collection centre and a detention centre I think it was, and you said that you couldn't see any difference. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said, but the premises for detention as regulated by law exist only within police stations, and this is where suspects are held, and for me in the jargon, in the unofficial language, the detention centre and the collection centre are the same. I don't see the difference in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. As you said, the detention centres -- sorry. The only premises for detention as regulated exists within police stations and presumably also prisons. Did you hear about prisons in Bileca being held -- prisons, I say, people being held in a place called the Dacki Dom?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I heard of it and I mentioned that name.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And some were called the Student Dormitory?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was pupils hall, not students. There is no university in Bileca so it was students as in secondary school students.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And people were being held there, you heard about that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I heard it from conversations and also from a meeting when it was discussed in Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Well, this is the next point I wanted to make. So that was the difference, wasn't it? That was clearly not a SJB premises nor a prison. So that was a collection centre, wasn't it? If that's what you call them.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never visited it, and I never called it, referred to it under that name. It wasn't a prison because later on the terminology was established and -- or rather it was done later whether they started calling it collection centres, then I don't know. At that time, back then nobody said to us there are this many people at a collection centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But these were not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, it appears that you aren't going to finish this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I am. I'll do it in two minutes so he doesn't have to come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Two minutes?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Two minutes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And as you said, you say you told Mr. Krgovic, I think it was Mr. Krgovic, that you never heard any official information about Bileca but you did actually, didn't you, because when you attended meetings, as you told us, in Trebinje you would hear reports on what was happening in Bileca.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was in that meeting when the representatives of the Ministry of the Interior attended.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But -- sorry, I'm just dealing with it. It's not right to say that the only information that you got about Bileca was private information?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I was trying to say is this: In the document, in the diary, you can see that there are meetings described and not in a single meeting was this discussed, perhaps just once.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally on this. Can you think of any reason why the head of the SJB, Mr. Vujovic, of Bileca, should be providing lists of persons over 60 who have been detained?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was a working group comprising two inspectors who did it. As I have said to you, I think that I know one of them but not the other one. These two inspectors are from the Ministry of Judiciary -- or, rather, could have been that the MUP submitted a report to the Ministry of Judiciary and this is what Vujovic said, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But would you recognise Mr. Vujovic's writing if you saw it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, because I never received any documents from him, and I haven't seen the man for almost 20 years, since 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's all that I ask. Thank you very much. Oh, yes, Your Honours. I'm reminded I didn't ask to have the document relating to war crimes exhibited, which he said he recognised the contents thereof. It's 65 ter 127.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P173, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krulj, we thank you for your attendance and assisting the Tribunal. You're now released, and we wish you a safe journey back to your home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, before we rise there's a question that we have of you, and we would seek your answer tomorrow. You would remember that in common with counsel from the other side and indeed the bench, it was recognised that it would be useful for there to be scheduled in advance days when we could all catch up with those things necessary to make our work in court more efficient, and it is proposed that the first of those days be Monday next, the 2nd of November, and that is dependent on how firm your arrangement is for a witness for that day but we'll take your answer tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll just tell you very quickly. We're so backed up now, Your Honours, that we've got three witnesses here at the moment. Monday would be not a particularly suitable day, I'm afraid, unless we would sent the witness away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we will resume tomorrow --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we fully appreciate -- we think it's a very good idea, but I think we need more advanced notice so that we can reorganise ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Tomorrow morning at 9.00 we resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 29th day of October, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
